text: The cure for a lonely heart is to be alone with Jesus.
explanation:
There's no misery like a lonely heart, and loneliness isn't about whether someone is beside you. You can be married and still be lonely; it's an empty heart. The Samaritan woman came to the well at noon to avoid people, and God arranged that even the disciples were away buying food. She was alone with Jesus.

Loneliness and aloneness aren't the same. Time alone with the One who knows everything about you and still draws near fills the empty place. Talk to Him about your day: when you're angry, tempted, sad. He loves to spend that time with you.

text: Nicodemus came to Jesus by night; Jesus went to the Samaritan woman at noon. He humbled the theologian and lifted up the sinner.
explanation:
Put John 3 and John 4 side by side. A respected male teacher of Israel versus a Samaritan woman with five former husbands. He came secretly at night; Jesus met her in broad daylight. He sought Jesus; Jesus sought her. He opened with "Rabbi, we know…" and was told, "You must be born again… Are you the teacher of Israel and do not know these things?"

But to her, Jesus wrapped the truth in compliments: "You have well said… in that you spoke truly." Every valley will be lifted up and every mountain brought low. Grace flows like water to the lowest places, so stay humble.

text: Most Jews took the long way around Samaria. Jesus "needed" to go through it, because one lonely woman was there.
explanation:
Travelling from Judea to Galilee, religious Jews would cross the Jordan and walk around Samaria rather than through it. But John says Jesus "needed to go through Samaria." The only need was a woman who had been looking for love in all the wrong places.

Notice what had just happened: the religious leaders in Judea had rejected Him. God's love doesn't turn bitter when it's refused; it simply goes looking for someone who'll receive it. If you think you're too far gone for Him to come your way, remember Samaria.

text: Jesus never told Nicodemus He was the Messiah. He told a Samaritan woman, "I who speak to you am He," literally, "I am."
explanation:
When the woman said, "I know that Messiah is coming… He will tell us all things," Jesus answered, "I who speak to you am He." In the Greek, "He" isn't there: "I am," the very name God gave Moses at the burning bush.

The great teaching on true worship, worship in spirit and in truth, wasn't given to a religious leader but to a woman with a broken history. She dropped her water pot, ran back to the town she'd been avoiding, and became an evangelist on the spot: "Come, see a Man who told me all things that I ever did."

text: Jacob prophesied that Joseph would be "a fruitful bough by a well, whose branches run over the wall." Jesus sat at Jacob's well, by Joseph's land, and blessed a Gentile.
explanation:
John notes that Sychar was "near the plot of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph," and that Jacob's well was there. Centuries earlier, Jacob had blessed Joseph: a fruitful bough by a well, its branches reaching over the wall. The wall pictures the separation between Jew and Gentile.

Jesus, the greater Joseph, sat by that well and His blessing reached over the wall to a Samaritan. And He did it while weary and resting. If He blesses like that when He's tired, imagine what He does now, strong and seated at the Father's right hand.

text: Numbers 21 hides John 3 and John 4 together: the bronze serpent lifted up, then a well where Israel sang, "Spring up, O well!"
explanation:
Jesus told Nicodemus, "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up." That's in Numbers 21. And in the same chapter, Israel turned toward the sunrise and came to Beer, which means well, where God said, "Gather the people, and I will give them water," and they sang to the well.

The serpent story happens, as it were, at night, like Nicodemus coming in the dark. The well comes after they face the sunrise, like the woman at noon. God hid both pictures of Jesus side by side, long before John wrote them down.

text: When your debt is paid, you can open the ledger and laugh. People who know they're forgiven don't need to be defensive.
explanation:
A businessman deep in debt can't bear to look at his accounts; it's all red. Then a wealthy friend pays everything off and leaves a surplus. Now he opens the ledger and laughs: "I owed that much? Look at that!" Every line fills him with gratitude toward his benefactor.

We get defensive ("You're the same!") when we're not sure we're forgiven. When you know the debt is paid, you can admit a fault freely: "It's not you, it's me. Pray for me." That's why the woman at the well could tell the whole town about her past.
